perm-064.title: The sea retreats and the reefs fail
perm-064.text: Ash beds date the end of the Middle Permian to 259.857 ± 0.084 million years ago, and at that moment the sea drained off the continents. The boundary coincided with one of the most prominent marine regressions of the Phanerozoic. Evaporites and land deposits lie over marine limestones, and a vast unconformity marks it in rocks worldwide. Falling seas and regional swings in salinity ended the golden age of reef building, in what is called the end-Guadalupian reef crisis. Closure of the Sino-Mongolian Seaway has been proposed as a driver of losses in the Paleo-Tethys. Global diversity, rebuilt by disaster species late in the Guadalupian, dropped again in the Wuchiapingian.

perm-067.title: The last callistophytalean seed ferns
perm-067.text: The Callistophytales were seed ferns whose coal forests had once covered South China. They make their last appearance in the Wuchiapingian, one more Carboniferous lineage gone before the great extinction.

perm-063.title: Dicynodonts and pareiasaurs flourish
perm-063.text: Beaked plant-eaters called dicynodonts became some of the most successful therapsids of all, surviving almost to the end of the Triassic. They flourished after the Capitanian extinction. Late Permian lands were dominated by advanced therapsids, saber-toothed gorgonopsians and dicynodonts, alongside large plant-eating pareiasaurs. South Africa's Beaufort Group shows the setting: a semi-arid cold steppe, crossed by seasonal rivers draining into the Karoo Sea.

perm-065.title: The first archosauromorphs
perm-065.text: Dinosaurs, pterosaurs and crocodile relatives all trace back to a group of reptiles that first appeared in the Late Permian. These were the archosauromorphs, which diversified before the period ended. The first archosauriforms appeared in the latest Permian. A molecular estimate puts the split of turtles from the line of birds and crocodilians at about 255 million years ago. A marine group of ichthyosauromorphs, sauropterygians and thalattosaurs may also have come from archosauromorphs in the Late Permian. Their real burst came later. Archosauromorphs exploded in diversity after the end-Permian extinction.

perm-066.title: The first gliding vertebrates
perm-066.text: Weigeltisaurids were lizard-like reptiles with extendable wings, like modern gliding lizards. They are the oldest known gliding vertebrates. Their worldwide spread shows that tall, thin forests, the kind a glider needs, had become widespread by the Late Permian.

perm-069.title: Rifting begins along the future Atlantic
perm-069.text: Pangaea's breakup can loosely be traced back to about 252 million years ago. From the latest Permian, a broad zone of stretching formed across the supercontinent along the line of the future Central Atlantic. Extension spread across Laurussia from central Europe to eastern Canada, opening north–south rift valleys.

perm-071.title: The Kupferschiefer, a copper-bearing black shale
perm-071.text: A layer usually only 30–60 cm thick spreads over 600,000 square km across six countries. The Kupferschiefer formed about 257 million years ago, when oxygen-free water in the enclosed Zechstein basin laid down a black shale and marl holding up to 30% organic matter. Mineral-rich groundwater later formed sulfide ores in it. It became one of the world's most important copper deposits, mined since at least 1199 AD.

perm-072.title: The Zechstein Sea lays down thick salt
perm-072.text: Beneath the North Sea, lowland Britain, Germany and Poland lies salt about 1,000 m thick. A rise in sea level, probably tied to melting ice, created the Zechstein Sea, a hypersaline inland sea. It sat near the equator in the rain shadow of the Central Pangean Mountains, and at least five cycles of evaporation piled up salt, anhydrite and dolomite. The sea's eventual disappearance was part of the regression around the end-Permian extinction.

perm-074.title: The longest icehouse ends
perm-074.text:
The final alpine glaciers melted in what is now eastern Australia around 255 million years ago. With them ended the Late Paleozoic icehouse, under way since the Late Devonian. It was the most extensive and longest icehouse of the Phanerozoic.

The ending was slow. The great southern ice sheets had shrunk long before, in the Artinskian warming, but cold returned in spells. A last regional glaciation, P4, lasted in Australia from the middle Capitanian to the late Wuchiapingian. Only then did the ice go for good.

By one account, the most recent greenhouse period began in the late Permian as this ice age ended. The timing matters. The world entered the end-Permian crisis already warm and ice-free, and {{ref:perm-082}} would push it much further.

perm-076.title: The Araguainha impact
perm-076.text: An impact left a crater 40 km wide on the border of Mato Grosso and Goiás, Brazil, probably in a shallow sea. Its age, 254.7 ± 2.5 million years, overlaps the Permian–Triassic boundary. Some suggest the warming it caused helped trigger the extinction.

perm-077.title: Salt fills the Delaware Basin
perm-077.text: Once the Hovey Channel was pinched shut by tectonics, the deep Delaware Basin of Texas and New Mexico was cut off from the sea, and its brines grew ever saltier. Up to 91 m of finely layered gypsum and anhydrite, the Castile Formation, settled in water over 500 m deep. Thick halite of the Salado followed. By the end of the Ochoan, the basin had filled to the top of the Capitan Reef and was mostly dry land.

perm-078.title: The Siberian Traps flood a continent
perm-078.text:
About 7 million km² of basalt still covers Siberia today, some 4 million km³ of rock. It is what remains of the Siberian Traps, one of the largest volcanic events of the last 500 million years. The eruptions went on for roughly two million years across the Permian–Triassic boundary.

The lava alone was not the main danger. Magma heated the coal- and evaporite-rich rocks of the Tungus basin, which can release large amounts of toxic and greenhouse gases. Carbon dioxide, sulfur dioxide, halogens and metals poured out. They drove warming, ocean anoxia and acidification, ozone loss, acid rain and repeated mercury poisoning.

Zircon dating ties the eruptions to the end-Permian extinction, and the traps are believed to be its primary cause. Each of the killing mechanisms that follow, from {{ref:perm-082}} to {{ref:perm-086}}, leads back here.

perm-079.title: The Glossopteris flora collapses
perm-079.text: In Australia, the Glossopteris forests collapsed around 370,000 years before the Permian–Triassic boundary. In western Gondwana they went probably a few hundred thousand years before it. These trees had dominated much of southern Gondwana since their order arose at the start of the Permian. Most or all of its members died out in the extinction, 251.9 million years ago. Just above the boundary, an Australia-wide conifer flora largely replaced them.

perm-081.title: A carbon signature of catastrophe
perm-081.text: Carbon atoms record the extinction even where rocks cannot be dated by radioactivity. A large, abrupt global fall in δ13C, the share of heavy carbon, coincides with the extinction and helps locate the boundary. Carbonate rocks worldwide record a swift drop of about 1% in the ratio of carbon-13 to carbon-12. The excursion measured 4–7% and lasted about 500,000 years, though altered rocks blur its exact size. Methane from frozen seabed clathrates was once the favored source of the light carbon. Isotopes now point mainly to volcanic carbon dioxide and methane cooked out of rocks by the Siberian Traps. Methane-producing microbes may explain some of the swings.

perm-082.title: The end-Permian hothouse
perm-082.text: Tropical seas off Iran topped 35 °C. The Siberian Traps released more than 5 teratonnes of carbon dioxide, more than doubling the atmosphere's share. Carbon dioxide rose from around 400 to 2,500 ppm as some 3,900–12,000 gigatonnes of carbon entered the oceans and air. Average surface temperature jumped from about 18 °C to as much as 35 °C. This rapid greenhouse release caused the extinction and began an extreme hothouse that lasted several million years into the Triassic.

perm-084.title: The Great Dying
perm-084.text:
About 81% of marine species vanished. On land, 70% of vertebrate species went with them. The end-Permian extinction is Earth's most severe known extinction, removing about 57% of families and 62% of genera.

It was fast. The main marine pulse took 60,000–100,000 years, and dating of ash beds at Meishan, China, places it between 251.941 and 251.880 million years ago. The consensus cause is {{ref:perm-078}}. Their carbon dioxide and sulfur dioxide brought global warming, sulfurous oxygen-starved seas and acidified oceans.

No group was safe. Shell-building marine animals suffered most. On land, it was the largest insect mass extinction, and it was equally catastrophic for plants.

The Great Dying ended the Paleozoic Era. Recovery was slow: land ecosystems needed some 30 million years to rebuild.

perm-085.title: Acid seas and acid rain
perm-085.text: The oceans grew more acidic by up to 0.7 pH units as carbon dioxide rose. That matches the pattern of loss, which fell hardest on heavily calcified animals. Acidification was worst at mid-latitudes, and together with anoxia a rising sea devastated shallow shelf communities. On land, acid rain lowered soil pH and sped erosion, washing organic matter from the land into the sea.

perm-086.title: Seas without oxygen
perm-086.text: Even the sunlit shallows filled with poison. Oxygen-starved, hydrogen-sulfide-rich waters, called euxinic, spread through the oceans from the Late Permian into the Early Triassic. Across most of the Tethys and Panthalassa, anoxia appears at the extinction itself, though at some sites it began earlier. Sulfate-reducing bacteria thrived and filled the sea with hydrogen sulfide. That gas, escaping from the sea, may have poisoned life on land and in the water. The extinction, triggered by runaway carbon dioxide from the Siberian Traps, was marked throughout by this loss of oxygen. Ocean overturn has also been proposed.

perm-088.title: Sea level swings at the boundary
perm-088.text: Global sea level is reported to have fallen 250 m during the Permian–Triassic extinction. The drastic regression shrank shallow shelf habitats and hastened the final decline of trilobites. Other work tells a different story, tying the main warming to a rise in sea level, which with anoxia ravaged shallow shelf life.

perm-089.title: The last spiny sharks
perm-089.text: The acanthodians, or spiny sharks, were an early class of jawed fishes. Their diversity had been low but stable through the Carboniferous and slipped further in the Permian. The Permian–Triassic extinction finished them.

perm-090.title: The last fusulinids
perm-090.text: Fusulinid foraminifera, large single-celled shell-builders, were already nearly gone. The Capitanian crisis had cut them down to dwarf forms. The Permian–Triassic extinction ended them. Lagenid forams survived, probably thanks to a wider tolerance of conditions and a wider range.

perm-091.title: The last gorgonopsians
perm-091.text: The top land predators of the Late Permian, the saber-toothed gorgonopsians, died out in the extinction's final phase. They began disappearing from Africa and Eastern Europe just before it. Biarmosuchians vanished too, while dicynodonts, therocephalians and cynodonts shrank to a handful of species each.

perm-092.title: The last griffinflies
perm-092.text: Several Paleozoic insect groups were extinct by the end of the Permian, including the giant griffinflies and the palaeodictyopteroids. Only three Paleozoic insect groups are known after it. This was the largest known mass extinction of insects.

perm-093.title: The last progymnosperms
perm-093.text: Progymnosperms were woody, spore-bearing plants thought to have given rise to the seed plants. Their last surviving group, the Noeggerathiales, persisted until the end of the Permian.

perm-094.title: The Paleozoic corals vanish
perm-094.text: About 96% of coral and other anthozoan genera were lost in the Permian–Triassic extinction. Among the casualties were the rugose and tabulate corals, the reef-building corals of the Paleozoic, which died out entirely. Their loss left the seas without the reef builders that had served them through the Paleozoic.

perm-095.title: The last lycopsid swamps
perm-095.text: Carboniferous-style swamps of lycopods and horsetails survived to the end of the Permian in only one place: Cathaysia, equatorial islands that became South China. Even there, tree lycopsids had become rare, marginal plants, no longer the main makers of coal.

perm-096.title: The last trilobites
perm-096.text: Trilobites had thrived since the Cambrian. At the end of the Permian, after nearly 300 million years, they were gone. Only one order, the Proetida, had survived the Devonian, and it lasted to the end. By the Changhsingian a handful of genera remained, by one count just two. Their final decline came shortly before the main extinction, as falling sea level shrank the shallow shelves where they lived.

perm-097.title: Pangaea dries out
perm-097.text: Near the end of the Permian, Pangaea grew drier as the supercontinent came together. Volcanism and global warming at the very end of the period sharply worsened the aridity. In Siberia's Kuznetsk Basin, drying killed the humid-adapted Cordaites forests a few hundred thousand years before the boundary.

perm-098.title: The impact idea, largely rejected
perm-098.text: Could an asteroid have caused the Great Dying? The idea is now largely rejected. Candidate craters include the 250 km Bedout structure off northwest Australia and a hypothesized 480 km Wilkes Land crater in Antarctica. Reported clues include shocked quartz, fullerenes with extraterrestrial gases and meteorite fragments. But iridium is not anomalous, and many boundary sites lack impact evidence. The proposed craters remain contentious, with their ages and origins still debated.

perm-100.title: The last sea scorpions
perm-100.text: Eurypterids, the sea scorpions, dwindled in numbers and diversity through the Permian. When they finally died out is contentious: either early in the Middle Permian or in the Permian–Triassic extinction, 251.9 million years ago. A cuticle fragment from the very end of the Permian in Australia, once called the youngest eurypterid, may instead be a scorpion.

openers.lopingian-epoch: The Lopingian, the last epoch of the Permian and of the Paleozoic, opened with one of the largest retreats of the sea in the Phanerozoic. Advanced therapsids ruled the land, from saber-toothed gorgonopsians to beaked dicynodonts, and the first archosauromorphs and gliding reptiles appeared. In Europe the Zechstein Sea spread and laid down black shale and thick salt, while the long Late Paleozoic icehouse finally ended. Then, in Siberia, basalt lava flooded a vast area, about 7 million km² of which remains today.

reviews.lopingian-epoch: The Lopingian ends in a single chain of cause and effect. The Siberian Traps heated coal and salt-rich rocks, releasing gases that more than doubled carbon dioxide, drove temperatures to as much as 35 °C and acidified the seas. Oceans lost their oxygen and filled with hydrogen sulfide, and the carbon isotope record bears the volcanic signature. The result was the Great Dying, which ended the trilobites, the Paleozoic corals, the gorgonopsians, the Glossopteris forests and countless insects. Impact ideas are largely rejected; the archosauromorphs and cynodonts that survived would inherit the world.
